clue.text: Intentions of the French, including gesticulation?

parts.note: de is the French word for 'of'
gesticulation is communicating by signs made with the hands

explanation.surface: Someone tries to read what the French mean from their expressive hand-waving.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that gesticulation is being loosely equated with hand signals; 'including' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans or purposes one has in mind are what a person has designs on achieving.

clue.text: Mason's supposed to do this. Spade might help.

definitions.text: Mason's supposed to do this. Spade might help.

parts.words: Mason's supposed to do this. Spade might help.
parts.note: reads like a builder at work with a spade, but A.E.W. Mason wrote crime novels and Sam Spade is Dashiell Hammett's private eye, so the job is sleuthing

explanation.surface: A stonemason is expected to dig, and a spade would be handy for it.
explanation.walkthrough: A.E.W. Mason created the French policeman Hanaud; Sam Spade is the hero of The Maltese Falcon. Both point to crime-solving rather than building.
explanation.definitionFit: Investigating crimes, as fictional sleuths do, means uncovering wrongdoing.

clue.text: Lumber and wood supplier for a Heart of Midlothian artisan

parts.note: to lumber someone with a burden is to saddle them with it
a tree is the source of timber

explanation.surface: A timber merchant supplies wood to a craftsman in Scott's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Bartoline Saddletree is the pedantic saddler in Walter Scott's The Heart of Midlothian; 'Lumber' looks like timber but is the verb meaning to burden.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddletree is the saddle-making tradesman among the characters of Scott's Edinburgh novel.

clue.text: Reg gets on horse that's bucking — a hunter

indicators.note: a bucking horse throws everything about, so the letters of the preceding words are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A rider called Reg mounts a horse that promptly starts bucking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's bucking' rearranges REG GETS ON HORSE. The hero of Siegfried Sassoon's Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man is the hunter meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassoon's fictional alter ego is a keen fox-hunting man, the central rider of the memoir.

clue.text: Owner of a circus organ in secret

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the word for secret, so 'in' signals the container

parts.note: sly means secretive, done on the quiet
the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: A circus proprietor keeps a musical organ hidden away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' suggests a fairground instrument but is the ear. Sleary runs the circus in Dickens's Hard Times.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Sleary is the lisping circus proprietor in Dickens's Hard Times.

clue.text: "The strongest of all warriors are these two — Time and -" (War and Peace)

definitions.text: "The strongest of all warriors are these two — Time and -" (War and Peace)

parts.words: "The strongest of all warriors are these two — Time and -" (War and Peace)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word completes Kutuzov's saying in Tolstoy's novel about the two forces that win wars

explanation.surface: A quotation from Tolstoy with its final word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: General Kutuzov says it in War and Peace: waiting, rather than fighting, defeats Napoleon.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the virtue of calm endurance and waiting, paired with time as Kutuzov's two warriors.

clue.text: In Forfar foretell an apse collapse

indicators.note: a collapsing structure falls into disorder, so the letters of the word before it tumble into a new order

explanation.surface: In a Scottish town, someone predicts that a church apse will fall down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Forfar' marks a Scots word: Forfar is a town in Angus, Scotland. 'collapse' rearranges APSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Spae is a Scots verb for prophesying, as in a spaewife who tells fortunes.

clue.text: His best-known work was about Sebastian and Andy, dizzy with love

definitions.text: His best-known work was about Sebastian

indicators.note: being dizzy leaves one's head spinning, so the letters of the two names are spun round into a new order

explanation.surface: A novelist wrote about two young men, Sebastian and Andy, giddy with romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dizzy' rearranges ANDY and LOVE. Sebastian invites Brideshead's Sebastian Flyte; he is in fact Sebastian Dangerfield of The Ginger Man.
explanation.definitionFit: J.P. Donleavy's famous novel The Ginger Man follows the roistering Sebastian Dangerfield.

clue.text: Has one sat in lap, like this dog?

indicators.note: these letters sit inside the word lap, so 'sat in' signals a container

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a means one
so means in this way, like this

explanation.surface: A small dog is asked whether one has sat in somebody's lap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sat in' makes the lap the container. The Lhasa apso is a small Tibetan breed, very much a lap dog, which gives the clue its picture.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-haired Tibetan breed is a small companion dog.

clue.text: Two people stand in front of the White House in this picture

definitions.text: Two people stand in front of the White House in this picture

parts.words: Two people stand in front of the White House in this picture
parts.note: suggests a presidential photograph in Washington, but the painting meant shows a farmer and a woman before a white wooden farmhouse

explanation.surface: A photograph of two people posing outside the President's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: Grant Wood's 1930 painting shows a pitchfork-holding farmer and a woman before a white Iowa farmhouse with a Gothic window.
explanation.definitionFit: Grant Wood's famous Iowa painting depicts a stern couple before their white farmhouse.

clue.text: Disraeli's Conservative little Eastern European

parts.note: a tad means a little bit
a Pole is a native of Poland

explanation.surface: Disraeli's Tory party apparently included a small man from Eastern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Tadpole and Taper are the scheming party hacks in Disraeli's novel Coningsby.
explanation.definitionFit: Tadpole is one of the Tory political operators satirised in Disraeli's Coningsby.

clue.text: First event in a Victorian fantasy book written by Emma Tennant

definitions.text: First event in a Victorian fantasy
definitions.meaning: the opening incident of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is the heroine tumbling down a rabbit hole
the title of Emma Tennant's 1980 novel

explanation.surface: Lewis Carroll's opening and Emma Tennant's book are run together as one.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's story begins with the girl dropping down the rabbit hole, and Tennant borrowed that phrase as a title.

clue.text: Suspicious Trollope character, later consumed with envy

indicators.note: something consumed is broken down and digested, so the letters of the two words are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A distrustful Trollope character is later eaten up by jealousy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumed' rearranges LATER and ENVY. Louis Trevelyan is the jealous husband of He Knew He Was Right, so 'Suspicious' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Trevelyan, obsessively jealous of his wife, is the central figure of Trollope's He Knew He Was Right.

clue.text: Help that's about to succeed in the end of a famous passage

definitions.text: the end of a famous passage

indicators.note: to succeed is to come after, so the reversed piece follows the word in

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: turned about, the word for help is read backwards

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: Assistance arrives just in time to succeed at the end of a famous journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the word for help backwards and 'to succeed' places it after IN. The famous passage is E.M. Forster's novel A Passage to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's title A Passage to India closes on the name of the subcontinent, its final word.

clue.text: Reworking of one bad oeuvre of a French author, really

indicators.note: reworking something reshapes it, so the letters that follow are reshaped into a new order

parts.note: the Roman numeral I means one

explanation.surface: A French writer revises one of her poor works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reworking of' rearranges I, BAD and OEUVRE. Oeuvre is French for a body of work, fitting Simone de Beauvoir.
explanation.definitionFit: Simone de Beauvoir was the French existentialist writer of The Second Sex.

clue.text: A granny with three bob to splash? That might trouble Greenwich students apparently

definitions.text: That might trouble Greenwich students apparently

indicators.note: splashing money about means scattering it, so the letters of the preceding words are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A grandmother with a few old shillings sets out to spend them freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to splash' rearranges A GRANNY THREE BOB; a bob was an old British shilling. Split as northern rage, the title is the pun: something to upset students in Greenwich, deep in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's Gothic parody, split differently, suggests fury from the north, a fright for southerners.

clue.text: One kind of handle for jug?

definitions.text: One kind of handle for jug?

parts.words: One kind of handle for jug?
parts.note: suggests the handle of a pitcher, but handle is slang for a name and jug is slang for prison, which has its own slang name

explanation.surface: Someone wonders which sort of handle suits a jug.
explanation.walkthrough: Handle is slang for a name, and jug and nick are both British slang for prison, so nick is an informal name for jug.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal or pet name for someone is a familiar alternative to the real one.

clue.text: "Physical diseases, engendered in the vices and — of men, will seize on victims of all degrees" (A Tale of Two Cities)

definitions.text: "Physical diseases, engendered in the vices and — of men, will seize on victims of all degrees" (A Tale of Two Cities)

parts.words: "Physical diseases, engendered in the vices and — of men, will seize on victims of all degrees" (A Tale of Two Cities)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word, a plural noun paired with vices, completes Dickens's warning about disease born of moral failings

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dickens with one word left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means failures of care or duty, set beside vices as causes of disease.

clue.text: Explicit novel by Nicola Barker

definitions.meaning: the title of Nicola Barker's 2004 novel about David Blaine's stunt over the Thames

explanation.surface: A frank novel by a contemporary British writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stated unambiguously is plain and transparent, and Barker used that adjective as a title.

clue.text: Story of a flood survivor finally prospering — in the tribe of Seth?

indicators.note: the final letter is placed inside the phrase for the tribe, so 'in' signals the container

parts.note: Seth is an Egyptian god, so his tribe is the race of gods; the question mark flags the stretch

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A tale of someone who survives the Flood and thrives, among the descendants of Adam's son Seth.
explanation.walkthrough: Seth suggests Adam's son, ancestor of Noah, but here he is the Egyptian god. Malamud's novel follows Calvin Cohn, sole survivor of a second flood.
explanation.definitionFit: Bernard Malamud's late novel tells of the last man alive after a new deluge.

clue.text: Disraeli is dropping reforming scheme to frustrate

indicators.note: the letters of the word is are let fall from the statesman's name before the rest is rearranged
reforming means making over again, so the remaining letters are given a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Disraeli abandons a programme of reform in order to thwart it.
explanation.walkthrough: Take IS from DISRAELI, leaving DRAELI, which 'reforming scheme' rearranges. The political surface about reform is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw a plan off its course is to thwart it, as a train is thrown off its tracks.

clue.text: A ship in literature — in part of the Old Testament

definitions.meaning: the refugee ship at the centre of Leon Uris's 1958 novel
the second book of the Bible, telling of the Israelites' departure from Egypt

explanation.surface: A literary vessel features in a book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Uris named his novel and its ship after the biblical book of the flight from Egypt.

clue.text: Clothing that may be rinsed in almost boiling water

parts.note: nigh means nearly, almost

indicators.note: boiling water churns, so the letters of the word water are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: Laundry instructions say these garments can be rinsed in water that is nearly boiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost boiling' reads as one phrase about hot water, but 'almost' gives NIGH and 'boiling' rearranges WATER. 'that may be rinsed in' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyjamas and nightgowns are garments worn in bed, a kind of apparel.

clue.text: The writer of a novella based in Vienna is back in Prague

definitions.text: The writer of a novella based in Vienna

indicators.note: read back, the run is taken from right to left
the letters sit inside the city's name, so 'in' signals a hidden run

explanation.surface: A writer of a story set in Vienna returns to Prague.
explanation.walkthrough: The run PRAG inside 'Prague', read 'back', gives the name. In John Irving's The World According to Garp, Garp writes the novella The Pension Grillparzer, set in Vienna.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of John Irving's novel is a writer whose first work is a Viennese novella.

clue.text: A quiet English novelist in the early twentieth century, a writer remembered for just one book

definitions.text: a writer remembered for just one book

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

parts.words: English novelist in the early twentieth century
parts.note: Ford Madox Ford wrote The Good Soldier and Parade's End

explanation.surface: A quiet English novelist of the early 1900s is remembered for a single book.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy Ashford wrote The Young Visiters at nine; it was published in 1919 and is her only famous work. The surface tempts the solver to take the whole first part as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Daisy Ashford is known solely for The Young Visiters, a novel written in childhood.

clue.text: Futurist bringing back computing, initially trying electrical nodes in memory

indicators.note: bringing the whole assembled string back means reading it from right to left

parts.note: IT stands for information technology, computing

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of each of the four words that follow

parts.note: RAM is random-access memory in a computer

explanation.surface: A tech-minded futurist revives computing by testing electrical nodes in memory chips.
explanation.walkthrough: IT, then TENI (the first letters of 'trying electrical nodes in'), then RAM are joined and the whole string is read backwards. The Futurist is Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the Italian art movement's founder.
explanation.definitionFit: Filippo Marinetti wrote the 1909 manifesto that launched the Italian avant-garde movement.

clue.text: Cast light in Rome on singular tribe of the ancient past

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after, so the abbreviation follows

parts.note: lucere is the Latin verb meaning to shine
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: Someone sheds light, in Rome, on a single ancient tribe.
explanation.walkthrough: The Luceres were one of the three original tribes of ancient Rome, with the Ramnes and Tities.
explanation.definitionFit: The Luceres were one of the three founding tribal divisions of early Rome.
